questions.topic: Meaning of a solution point of a linear system

questions.stem: A student graphs the equations y = 2x + 1 and y = -x + 10 on the same axes and marks the point (3, 7). Which statement best explains why (3, 7) is meaningful?

options.text: It is the only point where both equations have the same x-value.
options.misconception: Confuses matching x-values with solving the system.

options.text: It is the point where both equations are true at the same time.
It shows the y-intercept of the steeper line on the graph.
options.misconception: Mistakes the intersection for a y-intercept.

options.text: It proves both lines have the same slope as each other.
options.misconception: Believes intersection implies equal slopes.

questions.explanation: A solution of a system is an ordered pair that makes every equation in the system true simultaneously. Since (3, 7) lies on both lines, substituting x = 3 into both equations yields y = 7, so the pair satisfies both.
questions.hint: Think about what must be true for two equations at once, not just one.

options.text: There are infinitely many solutions because the two equations describe one line.

options.text: It satisfies only the first equation and not the second equation.
options.misconception: Believes a crossing point can satisfy only one equation.

options.text: It satisfies both equations of the system at the same time without exception.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Solving a system by eliminating a variable
questions.learningObjective: Solve a system by adding equations with opposite coefficients and report y.
questions.practice: Add equations to cancel a variable, then back-substitute for y.
questions.stem: A student solves the system 3x + 4y = 24 and 3x - 4y = 0 by adding the equations and is asked only for the value of y. What value should the student report?
questions.explanation: Adding the equations cancels the 4y terms and gives 6x = 24, so x = 4; substituting x = 4 into 3x + 4y = 24 gives 12 + 4y = 24, so 4y = 12 and y = 3, which checks in both equations.
questions.hint: Add the equations first so the y terms cancel out.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Meaning of a solution point of a linear system
questions.learningObjective: Connect a single solution to the graph relationship of the two lines.
questions.practice: Match each graph relationship to its number of shared points.
questions.stem: A system of two linear equations is solved and yields exactly one ordered pair. Which statement about the graphs of those two equations must be true?

options.text: The two lines intersect at exactly one point, which is the ordered pair found.
The two lines are parallel, and the solution lies somewhere between the two.
options.misconception: Believes parallel lines can share a single solution.

options.text: The two lines are identical, and the solution is the first point where they meet.
options.misconception: Confuses identical lines with a single unique solution.

options.text: The two lines are unrelated, so the pair comes from only one equation alone.
options.misconception: Ignores the requirement that both equations be satisfied.

questions.explanation: A single solution means a single shared point, which happens only when two distinct lines intersect once; parallel lines share no point and identical lines share all of them.
questions.hint: Match each possible graph relationship to its number of shared points.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Solving a system by eliminating a variable
questions.learningObjective: Apply elimination to a system and report the exact value of x.
questions.practice: Add equations so that one variable cancels completely.
questions.stem: A student solves the system 2x + y = 9 and 5x - y = 12 by eliminating y and is asked only for the value of x. What value should the student obtain?
questions.explanation: Adding the equations cancels the y terms and gives 7x = 21, so x = 3; substituting x = 3 into 2x + y = 9 gives 6 + y = 9, so y = 3, and the ordered pair (3, 3) satisfies both equations.
questions.hint: Add the two equations so that y and minus y cancel out.

questions.topic: Solving a system by graphing and substitution
questions.learningObjective: Solve a simple system by adding equations and report x exactly.
questions.practice: Combine equations and substitute back to obtain both coordinates.
questions.stem: A student solves the system x + y = 5 and 2x - y = 4 by adding the equations and is asked only for the value of x. What value should the student report?
questions.explanation: Adding the equations cancels y and gives 3x = 9, so x = 3; substituting x = 3 into x + y = 5 gives y = 2, and the ordered pair (3, 2) satisfies both original equations exactly.
questions.hint: Add the equations to cancel y, then substitute back for the other value.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Reporting the solution of a system
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a solution must be reported as an ordered pair.
questions.practice: Justify the standard form used to report a system's solution.
questions.stem: Two lines cross at the point (2, 6) on a coordinate plane. A student records the solution of the system as the value x = 2 alone. Why is this record an incomplete solution?

options.text: A system's solution is an ordered pair, so the y-value of 6 must be included.
The x-value of 2 is only an estimate and can never be a verified coordinate.
options.misconception: Dismisses a valid coordinate as unreliable.

options.text: Solutions must be written as equations, so the student needs to write y = 6.
options.misconception: Confuses the form of a solution with an equation.

options.text: The pair is only valid if the two lines also cross the origin of the plane.
options.misconception: Adds an incorrect condition about the origin.

questions.explanation: Solving a system means finding the ordered pair that satisfies both equations, so recording only x = 2 omits half of the answer; the complete solution taken from the graph is (2, 6).
questions.hint: Remember the form in which solutions of a system are written.
